question: What is the main goal of a Drug Revolving Fund (DRF) in a public hospital?

options.A: To generate heavy commercial profits for the government
options.B: To pay the monthly salaries of all medical doctors
options.C: To provide free medical care for all citizens permanently
options.D: To ensure a continuous supply of essential medicines

explanation: You've got this! A DRF uses money from selling drugs to buy more stock, making sure the pharmacy never runs dry. Simple and effective!

question: Why must the money collected from selling drugs in a DRF be kept separate from other hospital money?

options.A: So it can be used exclusively to buy replacement drug stock
options.B: To allow the hospital director to take a cash bonus
options.C: To pay off old utility bills owed by the kitchen staff
options.D: So the government knows how much tax the pharmacy owes

explanation: Spot on! Keeping DRF cash strictly for buying new drugs stops the money from leaking into other expenses, which is how stockouts happen.

question: What does 'self-financing' mean for a DRF scheme?

options.A: It generates enough revenue from sales to buy replacement stock
options.B: It borrows money from private banks whenever stocks get low
options.C: It relies entirely on yearly donations from foreign countries
options.D: It receives unlimited free drugs from the central ministry

explanation: Great job! Self-financing just means the fund keeps itself alive through patient payments instead of waiting for outside help.

question: Why are DRF drug prices kept lower than regular commercial pharmacies?

options.A: To ensure low-income patients can afford essential treatments
options.B: To punish private pharmacy owners for overcharging people
options.C: To make patients buy more drugs than they actually need
options.D: To drive private pharmaceutical companies completely out of business

explanation: Exactly! Public hospitals use DRFs to protect everyday people from suffering or extreme poverty just because they need basic medicine.

question: What is the very first step when starting up or running a DRF cycle?

options.A: Selling the expired drugs to local traders
options.B: Increasing the profit margin on all antibiotics
options.C: Writing off all debts owed by defaulting patients
options.D: Quantification and forecasting of drug needs

explanation: You got it! Before buying anything, you have to calculate how much medicine the hospital actually uses based on past patient attendance.

question: A hospital pharmacy keeps cash from drug sales in an open drawer and uses it to buy office snacks, leading to empty shelves. Which part of the DRF system is failing?
explanation: Makes total sense, right? If cash isn't banked safely and gets spent on snacks, the revolving fund stops revolving, and drugs run out!

question: Why is it risky to sell DRF drugs at the exact purchase price without adding a tiny markup?

options.A: It forces the government to arrest the chief pharmacist
options.B: It makes the pharmacy staff work extra hours for free
options.C: It causes patients to suspect the drugs are fake
options.D: It leaves no money to cover inflation, shipping, and wastage

explanation: Spot on! A small markup is needed because transport costs, damaged goods, and inflation will slowly eat away at the original capital.

question: What is the fastest way to crash and bankrupt a working Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: Conducting regular monthly stock counts of all tablets
options.B: Giving out large quantities of medicines on uncontrolled credit
options.C: Keeping the pharmacy store clean, dry, and well-ventilated
options.D: Buying drugs in large bulk quantities directly from manufacturers

explanation: You nailed it! If people take drugs on credit and never pay back, the cash never returns to buy new stock, and the fund collapses.

question: In a hospital pharmacy, what does the FEFO inventory rule stand for?
explanation: Easy and practical! FEFO means you sell the drugs that expire sooner first, so valuable medicine doesn't go to waste on the shelf.

question: Why do pharmacy teams do regular physical stock counts in a DRF?

options.A: To prove to patients that the building has air conditioning
options.B: To determine which medical doctor writes the most prescriptions
options.C: To ensure the pharmaceutical companies pay their annual taxes
options.D: To catch discrepancies between actual drug counts and record books

explanation: Great thinking! Counting physical items helps you spot missing stock, theft, or counting errors that paperwork won't show.

question: Which of these is a GOOD practice that actually protects a DRF, rather than harming it?

options.A: Bureaucratic delays in government procurement processes
options.B: Strict adherence to the FEFO inventory system
options.C: Political pressure to give out un-reimbursed free drugs
options.D: Internal staff pilferage and unauthorized drug taking

explanation: You've got this! FEFO is a smart safety habit. The other options (delays, theft, giving away free drugs) are threats that kill the fund.

question: How do long, slow government approval processes harm a revolving drug fund?

options.A: It forces patients to buy better quality drugs from abroad
options.B: It gives the pharmacy staff extra time to clean the shelves
options.C: It causes pharmaceutical companies to lower their wholesale prices
options.D: Inflation reduces the real purchasing power of the cash while waiting

explanation: Spot on! When approvals drag on for months, prices go up, meaning your saved cash can suddenly buy way fewer drugs than before.

question: How do accurate nursing medication records help support the DRF scheme?

options.A: They allow the hospital to charge patients double for every injection
options.B: They help pharmacists accurately forecast future drug consumption needs
options.C: They replace the need for physical stock counts in the pharmacy
options.D: They prove to the nursing council that staff are writing clearly

explanation: Wonderful! Clear records from the wards show exactly what patients are using, helping the pharmacy order the right amounts without guesswork.

question: As a nurse, you notice some IV fluid bottles on the ward shelf have changed color and passed their expiry date. What should you do?

options.A: Take the bottles home to use for domestic cleaning purposes
options.B: Hide the expired bottles in a bottom drawer so nobody notices
options.C: Administer them quickly to unsuspecting patients before they worsen
options.D: Report the expired stock immediately according to facility protocol

explanation: Safety first! Reporting expired stock keeps patients safe and ensures losses are recorded properly instead of silently disappearing.
